title: Diseases of the Placenta
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)

overview.intro: This chapter covers the diseases that arise from the placenta and its trophoblast: hydatidiform moles, invasive mole, and gestational choriocarcinoma; preeclampsia and its complications; abruption, previa, and accreta; and disorders of amniotic fluid volume. Each is explained from normal placental biology, including genomic imprinting, hCG signaling, trophoblast invasion of the spiral arteries, the decidua basalis, and the balance between fetal urine and fetal swallowing. Board questions turn on a few mechanistic distinctions: paternal versus maternal genomes, villi versus no villi, painful versus painless bleeding, and too little versus too much fluid. Once the mechanism is clear, each finding can be predicted.
prerequisites: Fertilization, implantation, and formation of the placenta and fetal membranes (RE-1, RE-6)
Cytotrophoblast, syncytiotrophoblast, and the structure of chorionic villi
Structure and actions of hCG and the glycoprotein hormone family (shared alpha subunit)
Endothelial control of vascular tone: nitric oxide, prostacyclin, VEGF
Fetal kidney and gut development (UR-1, GI-1)

connections.how: Very high hCG from a molar pregnancy weakly activates the TSH receptor and can cause hyperthyroidism with suppressed TSH.
Abruption, HELLP syndrome, and severe preeclampsia release tissue factor or injure endothelium, consuming platelets and clotting factors.
Loss of VEGF signaling in preeclampsia produces glomerular endotheliosis, which explains its proteinuria.

connections.to: Congenital renal and gut anomalies (UR-1, GI-1)
connections.how: Bilateral renal agenesis and esophageal or duodenal atresia announce themselves before birth as abnormal amniotic fluid volume.
Moles show how the parental origin of a genome, not only its content, controls growth.

terms.def: The group of disorders of abnormal trophoblast proliferation that includes hydatidiform moles, invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, and related tumors.
An abnormal conceptus with swollen (hydropic) chorionic villi and trophoblast proliferation caused by an excess of paternal genome.
Containing chromosomes derived only from the father, as in a complete mole.
Parent-of-origin silencing of certain genes, so that only the maternal or only the paternal copy is expressed.
A cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor encoded by a paternally imprinted, maternally expressed gene, used as an immunostain to detect maternal DNA in villous tissue.
Trophoblastic disease that persists or invades after pregnancy, including invasive mole and choriocarcinoma, recognized clinically by persistent hCG.
Replacement of the muscle and endothelium of maternal spiral arteries by invading trophoblast, converting them into wide, low-resistance vessels.
Soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1, a circulating fragment of VEGF receptor 1 that binds and neutralizes VEGF and placental growth factor (PlGF).
Hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets, a microangiopathic form of severe preeclampsia.
The endometrium beneath the implantation site that limits trophoblast invasion and provides the plane along which the placenta separates after birth.
Abnormally adherent placenta in which villi attach to (accreta), invade (increta), or penetrate through (percreta) the myometrium.
The chain of fetal deformities and pulmonary hypoplasia that follows severe, prolonged oligohydramnios from any cause.

blocks.text: Normal development needs one maternal and one paternal genome because of genomic imprinting. Paternally expressed genes generally drive growth of the trophoblast and placenta, while maternally expressed genes restrain trophoblast growth and support the embryo. A hydatidiform mole results when the paternal genome is in excess. The trophoblast proliferates, and the villous stroma fills with fluid largely because a fetal circulation to drain it is absent or inadequate, so the villi swell into grape-like vesicles.

A complete mole forms when an ovum that has lost its nucleus (an empty ovum) is fertilized. In about 90% of cases one sperm enters and its haploid set duplicates, giving a 46,XX karyotype in which every chromosome is paternal. In the rest, two sperm fertilize the empty ovum, giving 46,XX or 46,XY. A 46,YY conceptus does not survive, so complete moles are never YY. Because there is no maternal genome, no embryo forms, every villus swells, and trophoblast proliferates around the whole villous circumference.

A partial mole forms when a normal ovum is fertilized by two sperm (or by a diploid sperm), giving a triploid karyotype with one maternal and two paternal sets, most often 69,XXY and less often 69,XXX. The maternal set allows an embryo or fetus to begin developing, so fetal parts, fetal vessels, or nucleated fetal red cells are present, but the fetus is abnormal and does not survive. Only some villi swell, and trophoblast proliferation is focal and mild. Triploidy with two maternal sets and one paternal set does not produce a mole, which confirms that the paternal excess, not triploidy itself, causes molar change.

The p57 immunostain turns this genetic difference into a slide finding. CDKN1C, the gene for p57, is expressed only from the maternal allele. Villous cytotrophoblast and stromal cells of a complete mole contain no maternal DNA and are therefore p57 negative, while those of a partial mole or a hydropic miscarriage are positive.

blocks.title: Complete and partial hydatidiform mole
rows: Empty ovum plus one duplicated sperm (most) or two sperm
Raised, usually less than with complete mole
blocks.caption: The parental origin of the genome explains every row: a complete paternal excess gives a larger, more active trophoblast and no embryo.

blocks.title: Reading a karyotype and a stain
blocks.text: Tissue from a failed pregnancy at 11 weeks shows some swollen villi and a few nucleated red cells in villous vessels. Is it a complete mole? Fetal red cells mean a fetal circulation formed, which requires maternal genes, so a complete mole is unlikely. The karyotype is 69,XXY and p57 is positive. Positive p57 proves a maternal genome is present, and triploidy with molar villi means two paternal sets. The diagnosis is partial mole. Had the karyotype been 46,XX with negative p57 and diffuse swelling, the tissue would be a complete mole, even though 46,XX also describes a normal female conceptus; the stain, not the karyotype, shows the parental origin.

sections.title: Clinical findings of complete hydatidiform mole

blocks.text: Almost every finding of a complete mole follows from two facts: the uterus is filled with a large mass of swollen villi, and that mass is covered by proliferating syncytiotrophoblast that secretes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). The classic patient presents with vaginal bleeding in the first half of pregnancy, often late in the first trimester or early in the second. The bleeding comes from separation of molar tissue from the decidua, and over time it can cause anemia. The uterus is often larger than expected for the gestational age because of the volume of hydropic villi, and no fetal heart activity is found. Ultrasound shows a heterogeneous intrauterine mass with many small cystic spaces, described as a snowstorm pattern, and no fetus.

hCG is often above 100,000 mIU/mL. That value overlaps the normal peak at about 8 to 10 weeks, so a single level is suggestive rather than diagnostic; a level far above that expected for the gestational age, or one that keeps rising after the normal peak, is the useful signal. hCG is a glycoprotein hormone whose alpha subunit is shared with LH, FSH, and TSH, and whose beta subunit closely resembles that of LH, so at very high concentration it acts on related receptors.

blocks.title: How excess hCG produces the systemic findings
steps: Diffuse trophoblast proliferation secretes very large amounts of hCG
hCG binds LH/hCG receptors on ovarian theca cells
Bilateral, multilocular theca lutein cysts enlarge the ovaries
hCG weakly activates the structurally related TSH receptor
Thyroid hormone rises and TSH is suppressed (hyperthyroidism)
High hCG with estrogen is associated with hyperemesis gravidarum
blocks.caption: Theca lutein cysts and hyperthyroidism regress as hCG falls after the mole is removed. The link between hCG and vomiting is an association; its exact mechanism is not settled.

blocks.text: Preeclampsia that appears before 20 weeks of gestation strongly suggests a molar pregnancy. Ordinary preeclampsia waits until the second half of pregnancy, but the abnormal, oversized trophoblast mass of a mole releases antiangiogenic factors early, producing maternal endothelial dysfunction ahead of schedule through the mechanism explained in the section on the pathogenesis of preeclampsia.

The final consequence is malignant potential. Diffuse, unrestrained trophoblast proliferation is the substrate for invasive mole and choriocarcinoma, so after evacuation serial hCG measurements must fall to undetectable levels. A plateau or rise means trophoblast persists. Early ultrasound now detects many complete moles before this classic picture develops.

blocks.predict: Would a partial mole be expected to cause theca lutein cysts and hyperthyroidism as often as a complete mole?
blocks.explain: No. A partial mole has focal, mild trophoblast proliferation and lower hCG, so receptor cross-stimulation is uncommon, and the uterus is more often normal or small for dates.
blocks.check: Compare the hCG and trophoblast rows of the complete versus partial mole table with the flow in this section.

blocks.text: Normal trophoblast invades the decidua and the inner myometrium during implantation, but that invasion is controlled. An invasive mole is a hydatidiform mole, almost always complete, whose hydropic villi and trophoblast penetrate deep into the myometrium and its blood vessels. It is classified as gestational trophoblastic neoplasia because it persists and invades, yet it is not a carcinoma: it keeps the villous architecture of a mole. That single feature, villi present, separates it histologically from choriocarcinoma.

The consequences follow from where the tissue sits. Suction evacuation empties the uterine cavity but cannot reach villi buried in the wall, so trophoblast remains and continues to secrete hCG. Persistent or rising hCG after evacuation is therefore the usual way an invasive mole is recognized, and tissue diagnosis is uncommon because it requires a sample of the myometrium. Villi eroding through the wall can perforate the uterus and cause intraperitoneal hemorrhage, and those eroding vessels cause continued vaginal bleeding.

Because villi enter venous channels, they can be carried to the lungs or vagina. These deported villi are not true metastases in the sense of a carcinoma, and they may regress, but they keep producing hCG. Invasive mole follows about 10 to 15% of complete moles and is locally destructive rather than widely metastatic.

blocks.title: hCG after evacuation of a complete mole
blocks.text: A complete mole is evacuated and hCG is measured weekly: 150,000, then 40,000, 9,000, 8,800, 9,100, and 9,000 mIU/mL. What does the pattern mean? A cleared uterus should give a steady fall to undetectable levels, because hCG has a half-life of roughly a day and a half. A fall that stops at a plateau means living trophoblast remains that suction could not reach. With no new pregnancy, this defines persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. The most likely lesion after a complete mole is an invasive mole buried in the myometrium; choriocarcinoma is the less common alternative, and only histology (villi present or absent) separates them.

Gestational choriocarcinoma is a malignant tumor of trophoblast. It is composed of sheets of malignant cytotrophoblast mixed with syncytiotrophoblast (a biphasic pattern) and, unlike a mole, contains no chorionic villi. Normal trophoblast is built to invade maternal vessels, and the malignant cells keep that behavior. The tumor therefore grows into and around blood vessels, outgrows its own blood supply, and forms a soft, hemorrhagic, necrotic mass. A biopsy may contain mostly blood and dead tissue with viable tumor only at the edge.

Choriocarcinoma can follow any pregnancy event. About half arise after a complete hydatidiform mole, about a quarter after a spontaneous or induced abortion, and most of the rest after an apparently normal pregnancy, with a few after ectopic pregnancy. It may present weeks to years later with abnormal uterine bleeding, or first with a metastasis. Syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG in proportion to tumor mass, so hCG is very high and serves as a sensitive tumor marker.

Because the tumor lives within vessels, it spreads early through the blood rather than through lymphatics. The lungs are the most common site, producing multiple nodules on chest imaging with cough, hemoptysis, or dyspnea. The vagina is next, where metastases appear as dark, hemorrhagic nodules. Brain and liver metastases signal advanced disease and bleed readily, so a young woman with an intracerebral hemorrhage after a recent pregnancy should raise the question. Very high hCG can also cause theca lutein cysts or hyperthyroidism, as it does in a complete mole.

blocks.title: Distinguishing the trophoblastic lesions
rows: Hemorrhagic metastases to lung, vagina, brain
blocks.caption: Presence or absence of villi is the histologic dividing line between molar disease and choriocarcinoma; hCG tracks trophoblast mass in all four.

blocks.text: Gestational choriocarcinoma must be distinguished from nongestational choriocarcinoma, a germ cell tumor of the ovary or testis that arises from the patient's own cells. The gestational tumor carries paternal DNA from the pregnancy that produced it, while the nongestational tumor does not. The distinction matters because the gestational form has a much better prognosis despite its early spread.

Maternal blood reaches the placenta through spiral arteries, the terminal branches of the uterine arterial tree (uterine, arcuate, radial, then spiral). In normal pregnancy, extravillous cytotrophoblast migrates into these arteries, replaces their endothelium and smooth muscle, and leaves wide, flaccid channels that no longer constrict. This remodeling, which extends from the decidua into the inner myometrium during the first half of pregnancy, turns a high-resistance, pulsatile supply into a low-resistance, steady flow into the intervillous space.

In preeclampsia, invasion is shallow. The myometrial segments of the spiral arteries keep their muscle and stay narrow and reactive. The causes are incompletely understood, but they include abnormal maternal immune tolerance of trophoblast (interactions between uterine natural killer cells and fetal HLA molecules) and the inability of trophoblast to adopt the endothelial-like adhesion molecules needed to line vessels. The narrow arteries also develop acute atherosis, fibrinoid necrosis of the wall with lipid-laden macrophages, which narrows them further. The result is placental hypoperfusion, intermittent hypoxia and reoxygenation, and oxidative stress, seen in the placenta as infarcts and small villi.

This first, placental stage produces the second, maternal stage. The stressed syncytiotrophoblast releases large amounts of sFlt-1, which binds VEGF and placental growth factor (PlGF), and soluble endoglin, which binds TGF-beta. Maternal endothelial cells depend on VEGF and TGF-beta signaling to make nitric oxide and prostacyclin and to maintain the fenestrated endothelium of the glomeruli and hepatic sinusoids. Deprived of these signals, the endothelium shifts toward vasoconstriction and coagulation, with more thromboxane A2 and endothelin-1, increased sensitivity to angiotensin II, and leaky capillaries. In the kidney, glomerular endothelial cells swell and occlude the capillary lumens (glomerular endotheliosis), which reduces filtration and causes proteinuria.

blocks.title: Two-stage model of preeclampsia
steps: Shallow trophoblast invasion; spiral arteries stay narrow and muscular
Placental hypoperfusion, hypoxia and reoxygenation, oxidative stress
Placenta releases sFlt-1 and soluble endoglin into maternal blood
Free VEGF, PlGF, and TGF-beta signaling fall
Less nitric oxide and prostacyclin; more thromboxane and endothelin
Vasoconstriction, capillary leak, platelet activation, glomerular endotheliosis
Hypertension, proteinuria, and end-organ injury
blocks.caption: Stage 1 (first two steps) occurs in the placenta early in pregnancy and is clinically silent; stage 2 is the maternal syndrome after 20 weeks.

blocks.text: The model explains why the disease resolves after delivery of the placenta, why it is more frequent with a large placental mass (multiple gestation, molar pregnancy), and why maternal vascular disease (chronic hypertension, diabetes) adds risk. A high sFlt-1 to PlGF ratio in maternal blood reflects this antiangiogenic state and can precede clinical disease.

blocks.predict: If a woman with normal placentation were given a drug that blocks VEGF signaling, which features of preeclampsia would you expect?
blocks.explain: Hypertension and proteinuria with glomerular endothelial injury, because the maternal syndrome is driven by loss of VEGF signaling in endothelium; the placental stage is not required for these effects. VEGF inhibitors used in cancer therapy do cause this picture.
blocks.check: Compare with the third paragraph and the last four steps of the flow.

sections.title: Preeclampsia: definition, risk factors, and complications

blocks.text: Preeclampsia is new-onset hypertension, a blood pressure of 140/90 mm Hg or higher on two readings at least 4 hours apart, arising after 20 weeks of gestation in a woman previously normotensive, together with proteinuria or evidence of end-organ damage. Proteinuria is 300 mg or more in 24 hours or a urine protein to creatinine ratio of 0.3 mg/mg or more. Proteinuria is no longer required when end-organ injury is present, because the disease is systemic endothelial dysfunction and the kidney is only one of its targets. The 20-week threshold separates it from chronic hypertension, and preeclampsia earlier than that suggests a molar pregnancy.

blocks.title: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and end-organ criteria
rows: Hypertension before pregnancy or before 20 weeks
New hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria or end-organ damage
Milder or earlier stage of the same process in some women
New hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria or end-organ damage
Platelet activation and consumption on injured endothelium
Transaminases at least twice normal, right upper quadrant or epigastric pain
Periportal hemorrhage and necrosis stretch the liver capsule
Capillary leak and low plasma oncotic pressure
blocks.caption: Severe features include blood pressure of 160/110 mm Hg or higher or any of the listed end-organ findings. Thresholds follow current US obstetric consensus.

blocks.text: The strongest risk factor is preeclampsia in a previous pregnancy. Others either enlarge the placental mass or impair the maternal vessels that must support it: nulliparity, multiple gestation, molar pregnancy, chronic hypertension, pregestational diabetes, chronic kidney disease, systemic lupus erythematosus or antiphospholipid syndrome, obesity, and maternal age over about 35 years. Nulliparity is thought to matter because maternal immune tolerance of paternal antigens is not yet established.

Each complication is endothelial injury in a particular organ. Eclampsia is new generalized tonic-clonic seizures in a woman with preeclampsia that have no other cause. Sudden hypertension overwhelms cerebral autoregulation, and endothelial leak produces vasogenic edema, mainly in the parieto-occipital white matter (posterior reversible encephalopathy), which explains the headache and visual symptoms that often come first. HELLP syndrome is the microangiopathic form: red cells are sheared on fibrin strands in damaged small vessels (schistocytes, high LDH, low haptoglobin), hepatic sinusoidal injury and periportal necrosis raise transaminases and can cause subcapsular hematoma or rupture, and platelets are consumed. HELLP may occur with only mild hypertension. Severe disease can progress to DIC. The same narrowed spiral arteries that start the disease limit placental flow, causing fetal growth restriction, and arterial disease in the decidua predisposes to placental abruption. Stroke, mainly intracerebral hemorrhage, is a leading cause of maternal death in preeclampsia.

blocks.title: From endothelial injury to HELLP syndrome
steps: Injured endothelium of small vessels in liver and elsewhere
Platelets adhere and fibrin is deposited in small vessels
Red cells shear: schistocytes, high LDH, low haptoglobin
Hepatic sinusoidal obstruction and periportal hemorrhagic necrosis
Transaminases rise; capsule stretch causes epigastric pain
Platelet consumption: count falls below 100,000/µL
blocks.caption: HELLP is a thrombotic microangiopathy of pregnancy; the letters name the three laboratory consequences of one process.

blocks.text: Bleeding in the second half of pregnancy is classified by where the placenta sits and whether it is still attached. Placental abruption is premature separation of a normally implanted placenta from the uterine wall before delivery of the fetus. It begins with rupture of maternal vessels in the decidua basalis, and blood collecting between the placenta and the uterus (a retroplacental hematoma) dissects the placenta further away. Anything that damages decidual arteries or shears the placenta from the wall predisposes to it: hypertension and preeclampsia, cocaine use (intense vasoconstriction and surges in blood pressure), smoking, abdominal trauma, sudden uterine decompression after membrane rupture with polyhydramnios, and a prior abruption.

Each finding of abruption has a mechanism. Blood dissecting into the myometrium irritates it, causing pain, a firm or rigid tender uterus, and frequent contractions; severe extravasation into the muscle produces a purple, boggy Couvelaire uterus. Bleeding may be visible, or concealed behind the placenta, so vaginal blood loss can underestimate maternal hemorrhage. The separated area no longer exchanges gas, causing fetal distress or death. Damaged decidua and placenta are rich in tissue factor, which enters the maternal circulation and triggers disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), consuming fibrinogen and platelets.

Placenta previa is implantation of the placenta over or near the internal cervical os in the lower uterine segment. Risk factors are those that scar the upper uterus or make it less receptive: prior cesarean delivery or other uterine surgery, multiparity, multiple gestation, advanced maternal age, smoking, and a previous previa. In the third trimester the lower uterine segment forms and thins and the cervix begins to efface. The placenta cannot stretch with it, so its attachment shears and maternal vessels bleed. The blood escapes directly through the os rather than dissecting into muscle, so bleeding is painless and bright red, and the uterus is soft and nontender. The first episode is often small and stops on its own, with later bleeds heavier.

blocks.title: Causes of bleeding in the second half of pregnancy
rows: Decidual hemorrhage separates a normally sited placenta
Hypertension, cocaine, trauma; fetal distress; DIC
Placenta over the os shears as the lower segment thins
Bright red bleeding; prior cesarean or multiparity
Unprotected fetal vessels cross the membranes over the os and tear
Bleeding at membrane rupture with rapid fetal bradycardia; the blood is fetal
Tear through a scarred myometrium during labor
Prior uterine scar; fetal parts palpable outside the uterus
blocks.caption: Pain means blood is dissecting into or tearing the myometrium; painless bleeding means blood is escaping through the cervix without muscle injury.

blocks.predict: A woman at 33 weeks with preeclampsia develops abdominal pain, a rigid uterus, and only a small amount of vaginal bleeding, yet her blood pressure falls and she oozes from her IV site. Why?
blocks.explain: This is abruption with a concealed retroplacental hematoma, so true blood loss is much greater than what appears vaginally, and tissue factor release has started DIC, consuming clotting factors and platelets.
blocks.check: Compare with the second paragraph and the abruption row of the table.

blocks.text: At implantation the trophoblast invades the endometrium, which has transformed into decidua under progesterone. The decidua basalis under the placenta does two jobs. It restrains invasion, and it contains a layer of fibrinoid material (the Nitabuch layer) where trophoblast meets decidua. After delivery, the placenta separates through the spongy layer of the decidua basalis, and contraction of the myometrium then compresses the open maternal vessels to stop bleeding.

In the placenta accreta spectrum, the decidua basalis is absent or deficient, so villi anchor directly onto or into the myometrium. Without decidua there is no cleavage plane, and the placenta does not separate after birth. The problem is a defect in the maternal bed rather than overly aggressive trophoblast, which is why the main risk factors are conditions that scar or thin the endometrium: prior cesarean delivery, myomectomy, repeated curettage, and intrauterine adhesions. Placenta previa adds risk because the lower uterine segment has thin, poorly formed decidua and is where cesarean scars lie. The combination of a previa lying over a prior cesarean scar carries the highest risk, which rises with each additional cesarean.

blocks.title: Depth of attachment in the accreta spectrum
rows: Villi attach to the myometrial surface without intervening decidua
Placenta fails to separate; postpartum hemorrhage
Deeper invasion; heavier bleeding with attempted removal
Villi penetrate the full wall and serosa, sometimes into the bladder or other organs
Hematuria if the bladder is invaded; intraperitoneal hemorrhage or uterine rupture
blocks.caption: All three share the same cause, a missing decidua basalis; they differ only in how far villi extend.

blocks.text: Before delivery the disorder is usually silent, except for bleeding from an accompanying previa or hematuria from percreta. The dramatic manifestation comes in the third stage of labor: the placenta, or part of it, cannot be delivered. Attempts at separation tear open maternal vessels that the myometrium cannot compress because placental tissue remains embedded in it, causing massive postpartum hemorrhage, hemorrhagic shock, and consumptive coagulopathy. The rising cesarean rate has made the accreta spectrum much more common over recent decades.

Early in pregnancy amniotic fluid is mainly a filtrate of maternal and fetal plasma that crosses the membranes and the still unkeratinized fetal skin. The fetal kidneys begin producing urine at about 10 to 12 weeks, and from about the second trimester onward fetal urine is the main source of fluid, with a smaller contribution from fluid secreted by the fetal lungs. Fluid is removed mainly by fetal swallowing, with absorption in the fetal gut, and partly by absorption across the fetal surface of the placenta into fetal vessels. Volume peaks at about 800 mL in the mid third trimester and falls slightly toward term. Abnormal volume therefore points to a problem with fetal urine production or outflow, fetal swallowing, or the membranes.

Oligohydramnios is too little fluid, defined on ultrasound as an amniotic fluid index below 5 cm or a deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm. Fetal causes are failure to make urine (bilateral renal agenesis, bilateral cystic renal disease) or failure to pass it (posterior urethral valves in males, urethral atresia). Placental insufficiency also reduces urine output, because the hypoxic fetus redistributes blood to the brain, heart, and adrenals and away from the kidneys. Rupture of the membranes lets fluid leak away. Drugs that lower fetal renal perfusion, such as ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs, act through the same mechanism.

blocks.title: Potter sequence
steps: Fetal kidneys make little or no urine, or urine cannot leave
Severe oligohydramnios from early in the second trimester
Uterine wall compresses the fetus
Flattened face, recessed chin, low-set ears, clubfeet, joint contractures
Chest compression and loss of lung fluid limit lung growth
Pulmonary hypoplasia causes respiratory failure at birth
blocks.caption: A sequence is a cascade from one primary defect. Any cause of prolonged early oligohydramnios produces it; pulmonary hypoplasia is the usual cause of death.

blocks.text: Fetal lung growth requires retained lung fluid and room for fetal breathing movements, so the lungs are the organ most damaged by long-standing oligohydramnios. The characteristic face and limb deformities are mechanical, not primary malformations, which is why they occur whatever the original cause.

Polyhydramnios is excess fluid, an amniotic fluid index of about 24 to 25 cm or more or a deepest pocket of 8 cm or more. The fetus either cannot remove fluid or makes too much. Swallowing or upper gut absorption fails with esophageal atresia (often with a tracheoesophageal fistula), duodenal atresia (associated with Down syndrome), and anencephaly or other neurologic and neuromuscular disorders that impair the swallowing reflex. In maternal diabetes, glucose crosses the placenta, fetal hyperglycemia exceeds the renal threshold, and the resulting osmotic diuresis increases urine output. Many cases are mild and idiopathic. An overdistended uterus predisposes to preterm labor and, after delivery, to poor contraction and postpartum hemorrhage.

blocks.title: Causes of abnormal amniotic fluid volume
rows: Bilateral renal agenesis, bilateral cystic kidney disease
Urine cannot reach the amniotic cavity
Impaired swallowing or upper gut absorption
Maternal diabetes (osmotic diuresis), recipient twin in twin to twin transfusion
blocks.caption: Amniotic fluid volume is the balance between fetal urine in and fetal swallowing out.

integration.text: The trophoblast links every disorder in this chapter. Its growth is set by genomic imprinting, so an excess of paternal genome produces moles, and its malignant transformation produces a tumor that keeps the vessel-invading habit of normal trophoblast. Its depth of invasion is regulated from both sides: too shallow an invasion of the spiral arteries begins preeclampsia, while a missing decidua basalis lets villi invade too deeply, as in accreta. Its products act on the mother through ordinary endocrine and vascular physiology, hCG through the LH and TSH receptors and sFlt-1 by removing the VEGF that maternal endothelium needs.

The mechanisms also explain the limits of single findings. hCG is high in molar disease, choriocarcinoma, multiple gestation, and a normal pregnancy near its peak, so its trend and the gestational age matter more than one value. Painful versus painless bleeding is a good guide but not absolute, since a posterior abruption may cause back pain alone and a previa can bleed during labor. Amniotic fluid abnormalities are clues to fetal renal and gut anomalies that the embryology and urinary chapters explain in detail.

summary: A complete mole is androgenetic (usually 46,XX from an empty ovum and a duplicated sperm), has no fetus, diffuse villous swelling, and is p57 negative; a partial mole is triploid with one maternal set, fetal parts, focal swelling, and is p57 positive.

Complete mole findings come from mass and hCG: bleeding, uterus large for dates, snowstorm ultrasound, very high hCG, theca lutein cysts, hyperthyroidism through TSH receptor cross-reaction, hyperemesis, and preeclampsia before 20 weeks.
After evacuation hCG must fall to undetectable; a plateau or rise means persistent trophoblastic neoplasia, most often an invasive mole after a complete mole.
An invasive mole keeps villi but invades the myometrium, so it causes perforation, hemorrhage, and persistent hCG; choriocarcinoma has no villi.

Gestational choriocarcinoma is malignant cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast that follows a mole, abortion, or normal pregnancy, makes very high hCG, and spreads early through blood to lung, vagina, brain, and liver.

Preeclampsia begins with failed spiral artery remodeling and placental ischemia; sFlt-1 and soluble endoglin then neutralize VEGF, PlGF, and TGF-beta, causing systemic maternal endothelial dysfunction.

Preeclampsia is new blood pressure of 140/90 mm Hg or higher after 20 weeks with proteinuria or end-organ damage; complications are eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, abruption, fetal growth restriction, DIC, and stroke.

Abruption is painful bleeding with a tender firm uterus from decidual hemorrhage, linked to hypertension, cocaine, and trauma, and can trigger DIC through tissue factor; previa is painless bright red bleeding from a placenta over the os.

Placenta accreta spectrum results from a deficient decidua basalis, so villi attach to or invade myometrium; previa over a prior cesarean scar is the major risk, and failed separation causes massive postpartum hemorrhage.

Oligohydramnios reflects too little fetal urine or a leak and leads to Potter sequence with pulmonary hypoplasia; polyhydramnios reflects impaired swallowing (esophageal or duodenal atresia, anencephaly) or fetal osmotic diuresis in maternal diabetes.

verify: Diagnostic thresholds for preeclampsia (140/90 mm Hg on two readings 4 hours apart, proteinuria of 300 mg per 24 hours or protein to creatinine ratio of 0.3, platelets below 100,000/µL, creatinine above 1.1 mg/dL, transaminases twice normal, severe range 160/110 mm Hg) follow current US obstetric consensus; confirm the criteria NABNE uses.

Rates of persistent disease after complete (about 15 to 20%) and partial (about 1 to 5%) moles, choriocarcinoma after a complete mole (about 2 to 3%), and invasive mole after a complete mole (about 10 to 15%) vary between sources.
The origin distribution of gestational choriocarcinoma (about 50% after mole, 25% after abortion, most of the rest after normal pregnancy) follows Robbins; other series differ slightly.
The proportion of complete moles that are monospermic (about 90%) versus dispermic varies between older and newer genotyping studies.
The mechanism of hyperemesis gravidarum is not settled; hCG and estrogen are associated, and recent work implicates the placental hormone GDF15. Confirm what NABNE expects.

Ultrasound definitions of oligohydramnios and polyhydramnios (amniotic fluid index below 5 cm or deepest pocket below 2 cm; index of 24 or 25 cm or more, or deepest pocket of 8 cm or more) and the peak amniotic fluid volume (about 800 mL) vary slightly between sources.
The timing of the second, myometrial wave of spiral artery remodeling (classically about 16 to 20 weeks) is debated; this chapter says only that remodeling occurs during the first half of pregnancy.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Nitabuch layer, Couvelaire uterus, and Potter sequence or only the descriptive terms.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: mole-genetics (fertilization events producing complete and partial moles) and spiral-artery-remodeling (normal versus failed remodeling of the spiral arteries).
